div.p: Purpose -This study aims to offer the intellectual structure and dynamics of the sustainability branding field, involving the identification of influential authors and journals, current and emerging themes, theories, methods, contexts and future research directions. Design/methodology/approach -The study conducted a bibliometric approach of 1,509 articles retrieved from Scopus to analyze the evolution of the knowledge of sustainability branding and suggest future research. The analysis used various methods such as performance analysis, keyword analysis, cluster analysis and bibliographic coupling. Findings -The topics of corporate image, philanthropy and stakeholder pressures were core in the foundation phase. Then rose the topics of sustainable development goals and global supply chains. Green marketing and the new paradigms of circularity, ethical consumerism and hyperconnected societies emerged more recently. Six thematic clusters represent the field's knowledge structure: (1) corporate branding and reputation, (2) sustainable business development, (3) sustainable branding and ethical consumption, (4) corporate social responsibility, (5) brand equity and green marketing and (6) sustainability branding in hospitality and tourism. Practical implications -This paper provides readers with an overview of sustainability branding core themes, key contributions and challenges, which can be used as a toolkit for brand management studies and practice. Originality/value -The study's uniqueness lies in bibliometric analysis (combined with network analysis and science mapping techniques) of the sustainability branding field from the identification and evolution of the thematic clusters to propose future research directions.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Branding literature has evolved significantly over the past two decades. The shift from object (e.g. brands provide cues to influence product choices) to self-centered view (e.g. individuals use brands to express their desired self-identities) laid the groundwork for brand affects and symbolic meaning to occupy a central position. This is exemplified by the concepts of brand attachment (Thomson et al., 2005), trust (Chen, 2010), love (Batra et al., 2012), authenticity (Morhart et al., 2013;Nunes et al., 2021) and coolness (Warren et al., 2019). Brands achieved a wider social impact, amplified by hyperconnectivity and social media, creating communities and operating as relationship builders (Fetscherin et al., 2019;Fetscherin and Heinrich, 2015;Veloutsou and Liao, 2022;Veloutsou and Ruiz Mafe, 2019).
Sustainability and well-being are at the heart of this evolution. Brands seek to take a stance on important societal issues and expand their role (Golob et al., 2020;Swaminathan et al., 2020).

Unsurprisingly, the body of literature addressing these themes expanded rapidly in the marketing and branding context, as demonstrated by the prevalence of studies on proenvironmental and ethical consumer behaviors (e.g. Copeland and Bhaduri, 2020;Davies and Gutsche, 2016;Hosta and Zabkar, 2021), and the call for achieving a more holistic view of stakeholder value and societal concerns (Marketing Science Institute, 2022). Likewise, practitioners realize the importance of sustainable management for leveraging brand equity and achieving new competitive advantages (Kumar and Christodoulopoulou, 2014).

Given the impacts of sustainability on business, some studies summarized the current knowledge base on specific subthemes related to brand equity and corporate social responsibility (CSR) (Ishaq and Di Maria, 2020;Prasad and Kumar, 2022), but the The current issue and full text archive of this journal is available on Emerald Insight at: https://www.emerald.com/insight/1061-0421.htm overlap between sustainability and branding workstreams is not addressed. They are anchored on domain-based perspectives, not incorporating a holistic perspective (Veloutsou et al., 2022). Other reviews draw on conceptual, bibliometric or meta-analytical approaches (Bamberg and Möser, 2007;Groening et al., 2018;Nascimento and Loureiro, 2022), examining individual-level behaviors and do not address the impacts of sustainability on branding.
This study aims to address these gaps and provide academics and managers with a state of art and dynamics of sustainability branding research for advancing the field by specifically:

identifying key contributions and contributors, and assessing the development status; describing the evolution of extant literature and prevalent research contexts and focuses; illustrating its knowledge structure by categorizing and examining the main thematic clusters; determining which topics lie at the forefront of research; and based on those proposing future research directions.

The novelty of this work lies in its unique scope and suggestions for future research. The adoption of a predefined protocol ensures a robust and reproducible study of the vast body of literature. The bibliometric analysis uses an advanced set of network analysis and science mapping techniques (Donthu et al., 2021a(Donthu et al., , 2021b;;Mukherjee et al., 2022). The major study areas and approaches are synthesized and assisted by a guiding framework, which categorizes and presents a structured summary of the theories, contexts, characteristics and methods driving the field.

div.head: Background on sustainability branding
div.p: The organizational theories anchored sustainability in the "Triple Bottom Line" approach and the idea that corporate success is achieved not only by financial results but through social, ethical and ecological performance (Norman and MacDonald, 2004). Corporations began to explore how green supply chain management deals with stakeholder pressures to achieve competitive advantages (Laari et al., 2018;Wolf, 2014). As the focus turns to active engagement, case studies exemplified how sustainable branding stimulates co-creation and circular economy (Brydges, 2021;Morea et al., 2021;Scandelius and Cohen, 2016).

New organizational and social entrepreneurship concepts emerged, reflecting the blurred boundaries between ethical responsibility and business goals (Hota et al., 2020;Moroz and Gamble, 2021). Social responsibility broadens the view of sustainable development, showing that sustainable performance should not be divorced from economic achievement. Sustainable developmentdefined as satisfying the needs of the current generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs (World Commission, 1987) impacted management practices and scientific literature with major economic, political, technological and legal implications (Loureiro and Nascimento, 2021).

Sustainability was the focus of social and environmental psychologists concerned with the motivations of social and environmental behaviors, with some of the most important theoretical frameworks anchored on moral aspects (Chowdhury, 2017;Stern, 2000). The marketing literature examined selfaccountability and prosocial/environmental cues (Peloza et al., 2013;Sander et al., 2021;White and Peloza, 2009) to investigate consumption tradeoffs and the centrality of green and social/ethical features (Gershoff and Frels, 2015;Luchs and Kumar, 2017). Anticonsumption phenomena (Culiberg et al., 2023) raise questions about whether consumers really care and how they react to social responsibility or green marketing/advertising (Auger et al., 2003;Dangelico and Vocalelli, 2017;Pittman et al., 2022).

The concepts highlighted in the literature evolved independently and do not encompass a holistic view of sustainability (Appendix 1). How sustainability impacts branding is also unclear. Due to the vast and fragmented body of literature, a broader perspective is required for aggregating the multiple dimensions and disciplinary areas.

div.head: Methodology
div.p: The bibliometric analysis allows researchers to uncover implicit trends in academic production, giving insights for examining core themes and development paths. This study followed a predefined protocol (Donthu et al., 2021a(Donthu et al., , 2021b;;Mukherjee et al., 2022;Veloutsou and Liao, 2022), considering three steps for avoiding the limitations associated with bibliometric and review studies: identification of sources and data extraction; data cleaning; and data analysis.

div.head: Identification of sources
div.p: The largest collection of scientific research and the most complete metadata and citation information (Donthu et al., 2022;Veloutsou and Liao, 2022) justify the use of the Scopus database. The search query definition was based on the most salient keywords and search terms used in a pool of 27 review studies and meta-analyses related to marketing and sustainability. It was specifically comprised of the overlap between "brand"/"branding" (e.g. Ishaq and Di Maria, 2020) and "sustainab Ã " (e.g. Nascimento and Loureiro, 2022), "pro-environmental" (e.g. Bamberg and Möser, 2007), "green"/ "ecolog Ã " (e.g. Sharma, 2021), "social responsibility" (e.g. Prasad and Kumar, 2022) or "ethical consum Ã " (e.g. Groening et al., 2018).

The query was applied to the articles' title/abstract/keywords, resulting in the identification of 9,281 documents, from which 1,509 articles were retained for analysis. The selection comprised the following inclusion criteria: only articles in English and published between January 2001 and May 2023. Articles published before 2001 were excluded because "Triple Bottom Line" and individual-level behavioral theories development started around that period (Norman and MacDonald, 2004;Stern, 2000), which constituted the foundation steps to connect branding to sustainability issues in literature. Only journals from the "business, management and accounting" area were considered and outlets ranked below Scopus Q2 were excluded (Figure 1) to ensure an adequate level of fit and quality.

div.head: Data cleaning
div.p: Data were cleaned in terms of keywords, authors and journals (Veloutsou et al., 2022;Veloutsou and Liao, 2022;Veloutsou and Ruiz Mafe, 2019). Keywords were merged when the same term appeared with different spellings (e.g. behavior/behaviour), with single/plural forms (e.g. attitude/attitudes), and when different terms were detected with the same meaning (e.g. buying/purchasing). Vague terms with imprecise applicability (e.g. variable, fit) and overarching terms (e.g. sustainability, sustainable) were excluded to ensure a clear interpretation. This refinement ended with 5,160 unique terms from the initial list of 5,210 keywords. Next, the database was inspected to ensure that no missing values or data entry mistakes subsisted. The author names and affiliations were checked and, in some cases, were split or merged to ensure homogeneously coded records (e.g. Kang, Ju-Young and Kang, Jee-Won recorded originally as Kang, J. were split because they are different authors, whereas Apaolaza, Vanessa and Apaolaza-Ib añez were merged because correspond to the same author).

div.head: Data analysis
div.p: Bibliometric analyses often use performance analysis and science mapping (Cobo et al., 2015;Donthu et al., 2021aDonthu et al., , 2021b)). While the former uses evaluative techniques for assessing the contributions of research agents, the latter aims to display the scientific production's evolution and intellectual structure (meaning and structural relationships between the different research agents). This is illustrated through spatial representations of how documents, authors or research themes are connected (Donthu et al., 2022;Mukherjee et al., 2022). Both techniques were useful in combining the (a) identification of key contributions and contributors with the (b) analysis of conceptual relationships among them (Cobo et al., 2015), complementing the descriptive nature of performance analyses (VOSviewer, van Eck and Waltman, 2017).

Callon's centrality and density (Cobo et al., 2015;Courtial and Callon, 1991) represent themes' centrality and interconnectedness, indicating relevance (e.g. degree of interaction with other clusters across the network) and maturity (e.g. connectedness within its cluster). The thematic clustering technique used (keyword co-occurrence or co-word analysis) analyzes the conceptual proximity of documents by taking the authors' keywords as a proxy for the actual content's thematic focus, assuming that frequently connected terms are related (Cobo et al., 2015;Donthu et al., 2021aDonthu et al., , 2021b)). The clusters were positioned in a strategic diagram, a two-dimensional (2Â2) illustration of the development status of a given domain, with centrality and density measures represented in the axis.

Keyword occurrence and cluster data (21 years) were divided into nearly identical periods (Donthu et al., 2022;Veloutsou and Liao, 2022) to provide a clear perspective of how the sustainability branding field evolved. Clusters were assigned to the period in which 20% of accumulated network links occurred, signaling the influence of a specific body of literature.

Drawing on the Theories (T), Characteristics (C), Contexts (C) and Methods (M) (TCCM) framework (Bhattacharjee et al., 2022), the content of each period's most cited articles was inspected and categorized systematically. Regarding this framework, in each thematic cluster, the Characteristics are presented first, and then the Theory (T), Context (C) and Methods (M).

Finally, research avenues are presented in terms of areas and approaches. While research areas describe major themes and concepts, approaches address methodological and contextual focus in the literature (Veloutsou and Liao, 2022). The bibliographic couplinga mapping technique that groups documents citing the same sources (Donthu et al., 2021a(Donthu et al., , 2021b) ) facilitated the recognition of trends, gaps and shortcomings (Mukherjee et al., 2022).

div.head: Performance and keyword analysis
div.p: The data set (1,509 articles) contains 3,347 authors and 99 different journals and demonstrates the growing interest in sustainability branding (Figure 2). The most productive Inclusion criteria: articles only, English language, 'business, management and accounting' subject area. From the set of 5,160 keywords, a pool of 388 terms occurred four times or more and were extracted for analysis. Based on their occurrence frequency, the leading topics are CSR, sustainable development, consumer behavior, brand equity, social responsibility, brand image and advertising (accounting for 18% of occurrences). Thematic clusters are groups of keywords that are related to each other based on how often they appear together in the text (van Eck and Waltman, 2017). Six thematic clusters were identified and categorized (Figure 3 and Table 1).

div.head: Evolution of research and thematic clusters
div.p: The research clusters are characterized according to three phases. The main topics and concepts (characteristics) for each cluster are discussed first, followed by a summary of the prevalent theories, contexts and methods.

First phase (2001)(2002)(2003)(2004)(2005)(2006)(2007)(2008) Cluster 1: corporate branding and reputation. Sustainability was not initially considered a central topic. When the concept of CSR was introduced, it was mostly used for crisis management purposes (Klein and Dawar, 2004). Companies began to take proactive measures in response to stakeholder pressures rather than reacting to them. This is reflected in the initial research about the success factors of philanthropy and cause-related marketing. Findings show that CSR perceptions are more favorable for promoting causes (compared to elaborate advocacy messages) and elicit two main boundary conditions. When consumers are brand-conscious, and the brand's values align with their own, they tend to prioritize the brand over the social cause it represents (Menon and Kahn, 2003;Xiaoli and Kwangjun, 2007).

The strategic importance of sustainability branding grew, and new concepts such as eco-design and eco-labeling were introduced (Karlsson and Luttropp, 2006;Sammer and Wüstenhagen, 2006). Concurrently, retailers are often criticized for irresponsible practices, and a measurement scale was developed to assess corporate social irresponsibility (Wagner et al., 2008). The context was examined to explore the usefulness of certification and labeling, as well as how to leverage CSR or sustainability cues to enhance the brand image (Miller and Merrilees, 2013;Sigurdsson et al., 2023;Utgård, 2018). Overall, the social and ethical qualities of products are more valued by consumers than environmental attributes.

Even though this cluster has fallen into a declining status (Figure 4), charity donation (Mazodier et al., 2021) and causerelated marketing (Badenes-Rocha et al., 2022;Bergkvist and Zhou, 2019) are trending topics, raising important questions about whether (and how) companies are embracing them for strategic purposes. For instance, small Chinese firms use donations to mitigate the hazardous effects of environmental misconduct (Wu et al., 2021).

Theory-context-methods in Cluster 1: Organizational, stakeholder and attribution theories were important for laying the groundwork, with an abundance of grounded theory and exploratory approaches. Concerning research contexts, corporate donations and cause-related marketing in developed markets and highly regulated sectors were the main basis of the 2).

div.head: Second phase (2009-2016)
div.p: Cluster 2: sustainable business development. As e-commerce, global trade and supply chains expanded, a large body of literature discussed their impacts, addressing topics related to ecology, corporate ethics and stakeholder engagement. The involvement of a larger set of stakeholders, including internal actors and global suppliers, was discussed and important considerations were derived for sustainable operations. Sustainable branding was introduced as a means of unifying diverse corporate agendas and innovative forms of collaboration emerged as a result (Maon et al., 2021;Scandelius and Cohen, 2016). The domains of internal and employer branding gained expression (Carlini and Grace, 2021;de Chernatony and Cottam, 2006), with sustainability influencing a broader set of stakeholders.

Academics discussed new ways to meet customer requirements. First, the social responsibility of suppliers acts as a facilitator (e.g. logistic service providers and interorganizational packaging design) (Laari et al., 2018;White et al., 2015). Second, the entire organization should incorporate sustainable and responsible management principles, even if financial gains are not achieved in the short term (Brydges, 2021). Sustainable development was recognized as a global challenge. The relationship between sustainable supply chains and brand image determined the need to create new measurement indicators.

Theory-context-methods in Cluster 2: Organizational, signaling and attribution theories grounded most studies. Regarding contexts, researchers began to pay more attention to organizations in developing countries besides lean manufacturing and agro-industrial settings (Gandhi et al., 2018;Rueda et al., 2017). Multiple methods are often used with case studies and interviews as the predominant techniques.

Cluster 3: sustainability branding and ethical consumption. Academics explored the connection between sustainability branding and brand value. Corporate reputation, credibility and trust are core drivers (Chen, 2010;Hur et al., 2014;Olsen et al., 2014), yet the excessive usage of green messaging may backfire and trigger greenwashing concerns (Nyilasy et al., 2014;Parguel et al., 2011). This workflow connects to recent work about how familiarity can protect brands from unethical episodes (Nichols et al., 2023).

The willingness to buy/pay more for sustainable products and its determinant factors are core topics. Conflicting views subsist about the balance between proself and altruistic benefits (Nascimento and Loureiro, 2022). Attitudinal-based studies show how purchasing intentions toward socially/environmentally responsible brands depend both on sustainability features and product evaluations (e.g. functional, hedonic and aesthetic) and that sustainability outweighs self-interest only in specific circumstances (Hartmann and Apaolaza-Ib añez, 2012).

Moral/ethical and self-identity aspects are widely explored. Guilt shapes the influence of self-accountability as a key motive for ethical consumption (Peloza et al., 2013). An emerging area of particular interest is the contradictions between sustainability Note: CSR = Corporate Social Responsibility Source: Created by authors, using VOSviewer (version 1.6.17)

and conspicuousness (Aagerup and Nilsson, 2016). Consumer sensitivity toward sustainable luxury is relatively stable across cultures, but the underlined motives depend on individual affects and social and symbolic meanings (Kapferer and Michaut-Denizeau, 2014;Septianto et al., 2021).

Theory-context-methods in Cluster 3: Attitudinal-based theories were the norm for investigating sustainable/ethical consumption. Concerning the contexts, sustainable luxury, retail and organic products are core exploration areas linked with recent research about second-hand buying (Jain et al., 2022;Kim et al., 2021) and antibrand or anticonsumption activism (Pöyry and Laaksonen, 2022;Rahimah et al., 2022). Research was conducted mainly through questionnaire-based and experimental techniques.

Third-phase (2017-2023) Cluster 4: CSR. Earlier contributions examined firms accountable for considerable environmental/social impacts or operating in highly regulated industries. As CSR perspectives evolved, three main questions were addressed: (a) sustainable branding and CSR enablers, (b) outcomes and (c) typologies of CSR. The founder's role was uncovered as a facilitator for creating a sustainable image in two ways: as a cultural architect, energizing employees into environmental issues and as an eco-innovator, maximizing awareness and advocacy (Hillestad et al., 2010).

Regarding the outcomes of CSR, brand value is influenced by strategic and normative imperatives. While failing to meet societal and regulatory requirements (e.g. social irresponsibility episodes) may damage value in the short term, strategic and proactive action is the best way to improve brand valuations over a longer period (Agus Harjoto and Salas, 2017; Brunk and Blümelhuber, 2011). Customer engagement is a consequence of CSR-brand fit (Chuah et al., 2020). Brands benefit from adopting a proactive CSR approach to earn credibility.

Finally, new forms of CSR categorization were proposed, including multiple types (e.g. sponsorship, philanthropy and cause-related marketing) and dimensions (e.g. internal, economical and ethical). However, perceptions are not altered only on the basis of CSR typologies. The combined impacts of brand and benefit types are required to influence customer responses, with the effects regulated by individuals' social status (Lai et al., 2010;Lii and Lee, 2012;Wei and Jung, 2022).

Theory-context-methods in Cluster 4: With regard to theories, construal-level, value and attitude-based frameworks were frequently used. European, Asian and North American were the Notes: TL = total links (number of network connections); TO = total occurrences; APY = average publication year; TC/NP = number of citations per article; CSR = corporate social responsibility; SEM = structural equation modeling Source: Created by authors core contexts, with many studies examining cosmetic (Morea et al., 2021), oil/energy (Hillestad et al., 2010), fashion (Amatulli et al., 2018) and airline industries (Chuah et al., 2020). CSR topics are explored in social media contexts (Fern andez et al., 2022). In methods, experimental designs were prevalent, with the use of panel data and text mining techniques.

Cluster 5: brand equity and green marketing. Several brand equity frameworks were developed. First, a firm-oriented view on brand valuation described internal brand strength drivers, namely, associated with brand identity components, commitment and citizenship behaviors (Burmann et al., 2009). Second, identity-based views emphasize customer-level perceptions (Baalbaki and Guzm an, 2016). Authenticity is important for brands to resonate with customers (Huang and Guo, 2021). The consumer craving for brand heritage and authenticity emerged when analyzing successful approaches of small and global firms (Presas et al., 2011;Wiedmann et al., 2011), but recent findings suggest that dominant brands are perceived as less authentic (Wallach and Popovich, 2023).
With the rise of environmental activism and societal pressures, green marketing become a major theme in management.

Activities seeking to minimize the promotion (and/or impacts) of environmentally damaging products/services are adopted by marketers (Dangelico and Vocalelli, 2017). The key questions guiding research are related to the persuasiveness of green marketing claims, which were explored in two areas: the implications for (i) green buying intentions/behaviors and (ii) customer-brand relationships.

Similarly to CSR, the outcomes of green marketing are shaped by symbolic brand meanings. Green claims are insufficient (Guerreiro et al., 2023;Rosenbaum and Wong, 2015) unless brand perceptions are strengthened consistently. The premium price of many sustainable/green brands is identified as a barrier. Customers are only willing to pay more when the brand image meets their self-identity. New relational benefits were identifieddepending on relationship length and environmental consciousnesssuch as confidence and selfexpression (Papista and Dimitriadis, 2019).

Personal values, self-transcendence and altruism are important antecedents (Follows and Jobber, 2000). Universal values are associated with global lifestyles and connectedness in cultural identities (Salnikova et al., 2022)

Theory-context-methods in Cluster 5: Stimuli-organismresponse and identity-based theories are dominant. Several contrasting contexts were explored, namely, developed and emerging markets (Strizhakova and Coulter, 2013), multinational and family-owned firms (Presas et al., 2011), as well as service (Rosenbaum and Wong, 2015) and luxury brands (Kong et al., 2021). Concerning methods, surveys and experiments were mainly used in the cluster.

Cluster 6: sustainability branding in hospitality and tourism. The main question connecting this cluster is how to promote successful sustainable branding strategies for destinations. Community-based and ethical tourism experiences are identified as major trends for the future of the industry, associated with the popularity of authenticity and sustainability (Yeoman et al., 2007). The benefits of certifications were addressed, revealing not only marketing opportunities (e.g. recognition and reputation) but also environmental and financial gains (Jarvis et al., 2010). Resource allocation, time and knowledge are three relevant challenges in the implementation of sustainable strategies, and the lack of education is a major barrier.

Maintaining the desired brand meaning among multiple stakeholders is the focus of considerable research interest, with policymakers and academics pursuing different approaches and presenting actionable insights for brand cocreation (Giannopoulos et al., 2021;Reynolds et al., 2023;Tanguay et al., 2013). Effective actor-to-actor communication and shared values were highlighted as major building blocks for creating (and maintaining) destination brand value over time.

The ecotourism concept extended the cluster's connectedness and introduced new questions, such as understanding the role of psychological engagement and social media word-of-mouth (Chi, 2021;Quoquab et al., 2021).

Theory-context-methods in Cluster 6: As in other clusters in this phase, rational-based frameworks prevail, with some examples of other theories, such as institutional and service-dominant logic (Giannopoulos et al., 2021). Asian destinations were often analyzed, with an emphasis on green hotels, restaurants, city branding (Aitken and Campelo, 2011) and ecotourism (Chi, 2021). The analysis of methods indicated a balance between exploratory and survey-based studies.

div.head: Implications for future academic research
div.p: Taking a forward-looking view of the domain, future research avenues are outlined by identifying intellectually related workstreams through bibliographic coupling (Donthu et al., 2021a(Donthu et al., , 2021b)). Based on the most influential contributions and pressing research questions, the following areas and approaches (Table 3) are suggested.

div.head: Research areas
div.p: Strategic approaches for CSR and sustainability. A future challenge lies in extending multistakeholder approaches to explore how sustainable operationscombined with circularity and business innovationcan shape brand perceptions (Maon et al., 2021), connecting Clusters 2 and 3. Academics are encouraged to examine the broader concept of holistic circularity (Brydges, 2021). Similarly to green product innovations, further inquiries are needed to learn how to leverage green process innovations (Olsen et al., 2014).

Internal branding is an underdeveloped topic, as explored in Cluster 2 (Carlini and Grace, 2021;Muisyo et al., 2022). The perspective of stakeholders should also be accounted for, highlighting the importance of cocreation for sustainable place/ destination branding. Addressing multiple stakeholders (with distinct brand meanings) creates new tensions. As Cluster 6 suggests, residents are crucial actors operating as providers and receivers (Aitken and Campelo, 2011;Giannopoulos et al., 2021;Wang, 2019). The conditions that regulate their (dis) engagement due to over-tourism is a promising study area (Reynolds et al., 2023).

Creating value in a hyperconnected world through sustainable branding. Green marketing entails unknown aspects of online engagement to be investigated, as revealed in Cluster 4 (Kong et al., 2021;Swaminathan et al., 2020). With the exponential growth of digital platforms, social media became a predominant ecosystem for brands to signal their sustainability concerns. div.head: Contexts
div.p: Comparing developed to developing economies, and urban to rural settings, smart mobility and transportation, green services and energy, circular/shared consumption and peer-to-peer platforms, non-for-profit and cause-related marketing, small and medium enterprises, customer experiences powered by artificial intelligence, online sustainability branding Methods Mixed-method designs (combined qualitative and quantitative techniques), Web monitoring and content analysis, from correlational to experimental and choice-based conjoint approaches (e.g. from attitudes/intentions to actual behavioral responses)

Source: Created by authors (Sander et al., 2021). How to communicate social responsibility effectively in an online context (Fern andez et al., 2022)? Considering the relevance of new virtualized forms of brand-consumer interaction, further work should illuminate how its perceived authenticity affects outcomes and modifies brand meanings (Nunes et al., 2021;Pittman et al., 2022).

New paradigms for customer-(sustainable) brand relationships. Brand meaning influences customer appraisals (Diallo et al., 2021), but how do social, symbolic and functional meanings relate to self-brand identification? (Quach et al., 2022;Septianto et al., 2021). More research will contribute to understanding how consumers respond to socially appealing or high-status (eco-friendly) brands, as demonstrated by the evolution of literature in Group 3.

Conspicuous status signaling can result in negative responses, such as brand boycotting or avoidance (Table 3). However, delving into its emotional drivers could help clarify how antibrand attitudes trigger behaviors (Pöyry and Laaksonen, 2022;Rahimah et al., 2022). The topic of conspicuous anticonsumption also deserves attention to understand how self-expressiveness and social identities affect customer-brand relationships (Sekhon and Armstrong Soule, 2020).

Ethical consumers and circular economy. Ethical consumption is a crucial topic of discussion with significant questions for the future (see Cluster 3, Table 3). Peer-to-peer platforms, local products and other sharing economy initiatives have gained popularity due to the influence of sustainability values and online communities. However, brands still face significant challenges in leveraging the sharing economy.

Second-hand buying can be highly uncertain despite its many benefits. Future research could explore how storytelling and blockchain technology might alleviate risk perception by offering insights into the history of second-hand products (Jain et al., 2022;Kim et al., 2021). Cause-related marketing is another promising area for conceptual development, integrating advocacy and authenticity themes (Badenes-Rocha et al., 2022;Bergkvist and Zhou, 2019), which expands on cause-brand congruence and other core concepts introduced in Cluster 1.

div.head: Research approaches
div.p: Although a wide range of studies focuses on electric vehicles, organic products and sustainable tourism, there is still an opportunity to investigate deeper in these categories. For example, to unveil the ambivalences of electric mobility and shared ownership, considering nonenvironmental gains (e.g. convenience, cost and social value), or to compare organic and local product evaluations. Given the focus on large companies, fashion/luxury and cool brands, researchers should also examine small/medium enterprises and uncool categories to understand how to signal sustainability in functional and/or low-involvement choices (e.g. foods, personal care and green energy). Highly exposed (e.g. retail and public) and nonprofit sectors constitute other interesting contexts.

Further research opportunities lie in understanding the transformation of customer experiences, where sustainability concerns meet technological disruption driven by artificial intelligence and the metaverse. More attention can be given to service brands, exploring how responses to sustainability cues differ across online (vs offline) and robot (vs human-to-human) interactions.

Regarding the research methods, academics should try to overcome the existing shortcomings in sustainability branding literature and consider (a) using mixed-method research designs involving qualitative and experimental fieldwork and (b) addressing the limitations of correlational studies. These approaches are advised, for instance, for observing how to make sustainability claims more effective in advertising and packaging stimuli. In addition, based on the prevalence of social media, a combination of these techniques with Web content monitoring and text mining tools is recommended (Table 3), particularly to explore the new phenomena of virtual brand (and antibrand) communities. There are also relatively few studies using conjoint analysis, which would be appropriate for uncovering the weight of ethical/sustainable attributes in consumer choices.

div.head: Conclusion and limitations
div.p: This study embarked on a bibliometric analysis to explore the sustainability branding field, identifying the main contributors, emerging cluster themes and offering its intellectual structure. As climate change and corporate ethics have become increasingly prominent in media narratives and public discourse, research on sustainability branding has also gained interest. Particularly, sustainability, sustainable development, CSR and green branding topics are instrumental in developing the network's connectedness, whereas green marketing and brand equity are two frequently discussed and highly interconnected concepts driving the latest research. Digital disruption, circular economy and co-creation phenomenacombined with new forms of stakeholder involvementpose other interesting new avenues for future work. Although this study has made valuable contributions, it is not free from limitations. First, the analysis is based on bibliographic metadata, mainly the number of publications, citations or cocitations and keyword occurrence frequency, which implies that some topics may receive comparatively more attention than others, disregarding their theoretical significance. Second, the search query could be improved, as articles that do not mention the selected terms explicitly in their title, abstract or keywords were not considered. Finally, the data set considers only peer-reviewed articles. Other documents may be identified and examined in future studies.

div.head: Green brand
div.p: The specific set of perceived benefits and attributes related to the reduced environmental impact of that brand Consumer preference for green brands implied that such products/services earn a premium price, as brands started to use proenvironmental claims in marketing communications Papista and Krystallis (2019) Green marketing Marketing activities that attempt to reduce the perception of negative environmental impacts of existing products and production systems. Subdimensions: strategic, tactical and internal orientations

The green marketing orientation acknowledges that the firm's, consumer's and society's need to be satisfied in a sustainable and profitable way, compatible with the natural environment. Creates a new focus on maximizing green brand equity, by improving the brand's positioning/ identity and appealing to the audience's environmental concerns Dangelico and Vocalelli (2017) Green purchasing or buying behaviors

(1) Purchase of environmentally friendly products that are recyclable and conservable, as well as beneficial for and benevolent to the natural environment (2) Purposeful choice of products and services, intending to (or which may result in) reduced negative environmental impacts during the buying, usage, consumption and/or disposal stages (3) Purchasing practices that consider the environmental impacts of production processes, for example, purchasing recycled products or organically grown foods

The purchasing and consuming of products with minimal impacts on the environment, lead to a new paradigm that considers the environmental impacts of production and consumption (and consumers' own accountability). As a result, rapid growth in expected for market segments, such as secondhand and sustainable fashion, organic foods, green hotels and electric vehicles

div.head: Socially responsible consumption
div.p: Considers the public consequences of private consumption, and/or those who attempt to use their purchasing power to bring about social change (e.g. incorporate social issues into purchase decisions). Includesbut not restricted tothe evaluation of environmental consequences associated with the purchase of a product. Similar to "socially conscious consumption."

Consumers take into consideration the evaluation of the consequences of consumption upon society and the natural environment, as part of their decision criteria. Socially conscious consumers can be distinguished by a variety of personality, socioeconomic and attitudinal factors Follows and Jobber (2000) Sustainable consumer behaviors

Consumption behavior is based on awareness of the long-term consequences of an individual behavior for the natural or social environment Significant financial implications exist for the businesses involved, and an increasing level of consumer activism is observed (e.g. supporting organic products, made from sustainable materials or respecting fair trade principles, as well as boycotting firms accused of greenwashing or misconduct)
Hosta & Zabkar (2021)

div.head: Sustainable development
div.p: Meeting the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs

The United Nations' call for a more fairly distributed economic prosperity, and the urgency of balancing the ability of future (vs current) generations, as well as under-developed (vs developed) nations, to satisfy their primary needs, is changing the paradigms of business globally and becoming a central theme for brand management Wolf (2014), World Commission on environment and development (1987)

div.head: Sustainable marketing
div.p: The sustainable approach to consumption and production involves enjoying a material standard of living today, which is not at the expense of the standard of living of future generations

Addresses the business management processes and satisfaction of organizational goals, as well as the needs of customers, society and natural ecosystems. A profound shift is observed in business strategies, for creating new competitive advantages resulting from sustainable marketing as an opportunity for relevant differentiation and introducing a broader view of sustainability in management practices Dangelico and Vocalelli (2017) Triple bottom line (TBL)

The idea behind the 3BL paradigm is that a corporation's ultimate success or health can and should be measured not just by the traditional financial bottom line, but also by its social/ ethical and environmental performance
